name: Veerateeswarar Temple, Vazhuvur
deity: Shiva as Veerateeswarar (Krittivasar), with the Goddess Bala Gujambigai (Ilankili Nayaki)
period: Shrine of the Chola country named in the Tevaram (7th century); famed Chola bronze of Gajasamhara Murthy; one of the Ashta Veerattanams
summary: At Vazhuvur near Mayiladuthurai, Shiva tore apart the elephant sent against him and wrapped himself in its hide — the Veerattanam of Gajasamhara, home of a celebrated Chola bronze of that fierce and wondrous form.

sections.history: Vazhuvur is a village about 9 km south of Mayiladuthurai, known in older tradition as Darukavanam, the forest of the sages. Its temple to Shiva as Veerateeswarar is one of the eight Ashta Veerattanams, the one that remembers Gajasamhara, the slaying of the elephant. The village is named in the Tevaram, and the present masonry temple is assigned to the Chola period, with later expansion under the Thanjavur Nayaks. Its fame rests above all on its bronze of Gajasamhara Murthy, generally dated to the reign of Rajaraja I and counted among the masterpieces of Chola casting; here, unusually, that bronze is itself the centre of worship. A separate Veerabhadra temple stands elsewhere in the village.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan of the delta, its gateway and courtyards leading to the sanctum of Veerateeswarar, with the goddess in a shrine of her own. The heart of the visit, however, is the Gajasamhara Murthy: Shiva dancing upon the elephant's head within its flayed hide, which he holds outspread behind him like an arch, his many arms bearing weapons. Even by the light of a shrine lamp, the bronze conveys terror and grace together.
sections.legends: The sages of the Darukavanam forest trusted only in their rites and austerities, forgetting the Lord those rites were meant for. Shiva came among them as Bhikshatana, the beautiful mendicant, with Vishnu as Mohini, and their pride was shaken. In anger the sages raised forces against him from their sacrificial fire — a tiger, a serpent and at last a raging elephant. Shiva met the elephant, tore it apart and wrapped himself in its hide, and so he is called Krittivasar, the Lord clothed in the skin. Vazhuvur honours that victory over ritual without devotion.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri, the fortnightly pradosham, Arudra Darshan in Margazhi and Karthigai Deepam are kept through the Shaiva year, and the annual festival brings out the processional images; on special days the Gajasamhara bronze receives abhishekam and elaborate decoration. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Vazhuvur draws pilgrims and lovers of art alike. Devotees come to stand before the Lord who humbled the proud sages; students of Chola bronze come for the Gajasamhara Murthy, which many judge among the finest metal images of South India. Korukkai, the Veerattanam of Kama, lies a short drive to the north, and Mayiladuthurai's other shrines are close at hand.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the delta. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Vazhuvur lies about 9 km south of Mayiladuthurai and is reached by road, with local buses and taxis from the town. Mayiladuthurai is the nearest railway junction; Tiruchirappalli is the nearest large airport.
